sweep_summary: Tohono O'odham (toho1245, catalog fixed-strict initial, deciding source Zepeda 1983 p.3 pedagogical grammar). Six title-hits, all by the language's stress specialist Fitzgerald or by Yu, all about word stress of this language; none is noise. Read in full (open copies, listed): Yu 2000 Phonology 17 (author copy archived from his UChicago page, p.118 'Primary stress in TO always falls on the initial syllable, regardless of whether the form is derived or underived'; Spanish loans with non-initial stress treated as lexical), Fitzgerald 2012 IJAL 78 (UT Arlington OA deposit that OpenAIRE lists as the open instance, downloaded from the Internet Archive since uchicago and mavmatrix are could not be reached by automated download; initial syllable 'carries primary stress' / 'is the locus of primary stress', odd-syllable secondary stress regardless of weight, ~150 Spanish loans with non-initial stress and speaker variation), the published BLS 1994 paper (p.176 initial stress, ha- prefix and stative s- unstressed), plus the not-listed Fitzgerald 1998 IJAL 64 song-meter paper (p.5: 'a primary stress falls on the first syllable of a stem', citing Hale 1959, Saxton 1963, Hill & Zepeda 1992). Every read source confirms the catalog's fixed initial coding; the refinement is a lexical exception class of Spanish loans and proclitic person markers/stative s- outside the domain (matches the StressTyp2/Gordon 'root' wording already explained in the held Fitzgerald 1997 dissertation p.57, 85 fn.28). Not obtained: Fitzgerald 1996 WCCFL 15 (print proceedings; Yu 2000 says his data come from it and the 1997 dissertation; low priority), Fitzgerald 2001 Linguistics 39 (De Gruyter paywall, DOI 10.1515/ling.2001.039; medium), Fitzgerald 1999 Anthropological Linguistics 41 (JSTOR only, no DOI; page range disagrees between Glottolog 193-208 and Fitzgerald's own 2012 reference list 1-33; medium, since it is the dedicated treatment of the loanword exceptions). Related not-listed item: Fitzgerald 2002 Phonology 19 'Tohono O'odham stress in a single ranking' (abstract read, closed). Best new statement: Fitzgerald 2012 IJAL, first-hand and peer-reviewed, same coding as the catalog; recommended as an evidence-grade upgrade over the 1983 pedagogical grammar.

[p.440] 3.1. Alternating stress. Stress falls on odd-numbered syllables in O'odham regardless of syllable weight. Alternating rhythm and odd syllable stress favor a trochaic analysis of these facts. new_statements.citation: Fitzgerald, Colleen M. 2012. Prosodic inconsistency in Tohono O'odham. International Journal of American Linguistics 78(4): 435-463. DOI 10.1086/666930.
new_statements.reading: Primary stress is fixed on the initial syllable of the word, quantity-insensitive, with trochaic secondary stress on odd-numbered syllables (word-final secondary stress only in polymorphemic words). The stative proclitic s- and reflexive are set aside as outside the stress domain (fn. 5), and a small class (~150 in Mathiot 1973) of Spanish loans keeps the Spanish stress position as lexical exceptions (sec. 4.4.2). This is the same coding as the catalog's fixed-strict initial; the nearly identical crisp wording is in Fitzgerald 1998 IJAL 64 p. 5 ('a primary stress falls on the first syllable of a stem', citing Hale 1959, Saxton 1963, Hill & Zepeda 1992) and in Yu 2000 p. 118.

new_statements.quote: [p.113] The syllable is the unit of stress placement. There are three degrees of stress: primary, secondary, and unstressed. Stress is predictable, but for descriptive purposes, primary stress is indicated by (') ... [p.114] Primary stress occurs on the first syllable of major class words and parts of compounds, on any non-back vowel immediately following hu, ku, or wu, and on the first vowel otherwise, as in: Huan 'John', Huiwis 'Thursday', kui 'mesquite', wua 'to put (something) down', koa 'forehead', waid 'to invite', paal-wakon 'to baptize', etc. Secondary stress occurs on certain syllables with no primary stress. [p.144, Pronunciation Guide note 1] The stressed or loudest part of a word is the vowel following initial ku or wu, the first vowel otherwise.

new_statements.rule_in_words: The archive.org record at the listed open_url (micro_IA41153443_0463) is not the 1982 grammar sketch; it is the ERIC microfiche (ED 241 236) of Saxton, Saxton & Enos 1983, Dictionary: Papago/Pima-English, English-Papago/Pima, 2nd ed., University of Arizona Press, 174 pp. That dictionary's Appendix One 'Phonology' (pp. 113-115) does state word stress: three degrees (primary, secondary, unstressed), stress is predictable; primary stress on the first syllable of major-class words and of each part of a compound (where an initial hu/ku/wu is treated as an onset, primary stress goes on the following non-back vowel, e.g. kui 'mesquite', Huan 'John'; otherwise on the first vowel). The Pronunciation Guide (p. 144, note 1) repeats it in lay terms. So: fixed initial, quantity-insensitive, predictable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: p.114: 'Secondary stress occurs on certain syllables with no primary stress. On vowel sequences, secondary stress occurs on the first of identical-vowel, or high-low vowel, or interrupted sequences, and on the last vowel otherwise' (e.g. 'iidaa 'this', tohaa 'to become white', ho'ige'idaa 'blessing'); 'On single vowels, secondary stress occurs on the last vowel in a word that precedes a voiced consonant without a following stressed vowel' ('idagi, 'idagida 'to own'; hiwigi, hiwigida 'to permit'). p.115 adds a clause/phrase 'tone contour' whose level is high from the first through the last primary stress of the construction and low elsewhere.
new_statements.exceptions: Words beginning with hu/ku/wu: primary stress falls on the non-back vowel immediately after that sequence (Huan, Huiwis, kui, wua), i.e. the u is treated as part of the onset, so this is still the first syllable. Each part of a compound gets its own primary stress (paal-wakon 'to baptize'). No mention of Spanish loans with non-initial stress in this appendix (Spanish loans are discussed only for n/ng/y phonemes, p.115).
new_statements.identity_note: The dictionary covers Papago/Pima jointly (Tohono O'odham and Akimel O'odham/Pima) and notes one dialect difference in offglide phonetics (Totoguani treats d as a stop), none in stress placement. The listed work 0 (Saxton 1982 SUAG-3 sketch) was not what the open_url delivered; the quotes come from the 1983 dictionary by the same principal author.

sources.citation: Fitzgerald, Colleen M. 1994. Prosody drives the syntax: O'odham rhythm. Proceedings of the Berkeley Linguistics Society 20, 173-183. DOI 10.3765/bls.v20i1.1462.
sources.quote: In monomorphemic content words, primary stress falls on the initial syllable of the word (Zepeda, 1988). [...] In reduplicated words, stress falls on the reduplicant (still the initial syllable). All other prefixes (such as the ha-, third person plural object) are unstressed; the stative suffix s- will be syllabified with the following material [...] The generalization here is that the word-level phonology of TO prefers trochees.
sources.note: Primary stress on the word-initial syllable; reduplicant (still initial) takes it; ha- object prefix and stative s- are unstressed. Paper's main topic is utterance-level prosody driving syntax (g determiner, second-position auxiliary).

sources.quote: The basic pattern is alternating odd-syllable stress, with the primary stress falling word-initially. Final secondary stresses are allowed if a word is polymorphemic (1b), but not if the word is monomorphemic (1a). [...] It should be noted that long vowels are restricted to initial syllables, and in no way affect the generalisations about stress. [p. 254] || The basic pattern of stress shown in (1) and (2) consists of alternating odd-syllable stress, with primary stress on the leftmost syllable. The presence of stress on both initial and odd syllables signals a trochaic metrical system, which assigns stress using a quantity-insensitive left-headed foot, the syllabic trochee (Hayes 1995). Feet align from the left edge of the word. [...] All non-final feet are binary. However, since the monomorphemic and polymorphemic words contrast in whether they allow a final secondary stress, the final syllable may be either stressed in a degenerate foot, as in (pi-pi)(ba) 'pipe PL', or unstressed and unfooted, as in (musi)go 'musician'. This is determined according to the morphological structure of the word, and is relevant only for words that consist of an odd number of syllables. [p. 256]

sources.quote: Primary stress in TO always falls on the initial syllable, regardless of whether the form is derived or underived.1 The distribution of stress in underived forms is shown in (1). No secondary stress is assigned to disyllabic and trisyllabic underived words (1b, c), but secondary stresses are assigned to the odd-numbered syllables of polysyllabic words as long as the syllable is non-final (1d). [fn.1] There is also a class of Spanish loans with non-initial primary stress. I assume that these forms have lexical stress and I will have nothing to say about them in this paper.
sources.note: Primary stress always word-initial (on the reduplicant when reduplicated), secondary stress on odd syllables with final secondary stress only in derived words (the NDEB case the paper analyzes via co-phonologies); data are taken from Fitzgerald 1996/1997, so second-hand.

sources.access_detail: online with restricted access (login, paywall or limited view)
sources.note: Sentence intonation is entirely predictable from surface syntax: the sentence is parsed into one or more tonal phrases, each assigned the melody (L)HL (H spanning from the first stressed syllable to the last primary stress, L after; optional initial L on unstressed material), with tonal-phrase edges determined by government/maximal projections. I.e. pitch is post-lexical phrasal tone, no lexical tone contrast; the classic source for O'odham 'tonal phrasing' used in later syntax-prosody work (Truckenbrodt 1999 etc.).

tone.quote: The intonation contour of a Papago sentence is entirely predictable on the basis of its surface syntactic structure. It consists of a sequence of instances of the pattern (L)HL. [...] Our analysis is that the phonological representation of a sentence of Papago consists of a sequence of one or more tonal phrases, and that (L)HL is the pattern assigned to a tonal phrase. [...] The association of the (L)HL pattern within each tonal phrase is captured by simple rules of the phonology, to be described in §2.

sources.note: No lexical tone; a predictable clause/phrase-level 'tone contour': pitch is high from the first through the last primary stress of the main part of each clause or phrase and low elsewhere (same rule as Saxton 1982 sketch p.101 'Raise pitch from first stressed syllable through last primary stress in each clause and phrase predicate'). Stress itself is predictable (three degrees; primary on first syllable of major-class words).
